Documentation → Plugin Studio: build your own → SATOM Builder path

Build with SATOM Builder, from zero

The whole path with SATOM Builder — install it, link it to SATOM with a token, create a project, pick datasets, start from SATOM's own data, explore it as a database with a diagram and SQL, ask the assistant, test-run with SATOM's own runtime, and send the package to a test SATOM and then production.

👤 ForAdministratorAdvanced user
🔑 Permissionsstudio.script_library studio.plugin_studio
📍 WhereSATOM Builder (a separate server) ↔ SATOM /api/v1/builder/*

Why SATOM Builder#

SATOM Builder is a separate tool, installed by you on its own server, for building plugins away from your production SATOM: it checks packages with SATOM's own rules, renders views and walks diagrams with SATOM's own code on test data, runs scripts in the same jail, keeps an AI assistant conversation per project, and sends the finished package to a SATOM. It talks to SATOM only through /api/v1/builder/*, with each author's own token, so it sees exactly what that author may see.

Step 1 — install and link it#

  1. Install SATOM Builder on its own server (its installer, or the offline bundles from the downloads page). It needs SATOM 4.3.0 or later for every dataset and test data from SATOM (4.2.0 for test runs and the library).
  2. In SATOM, create an API token for each author: scope read to fetch the target and its data, write to validate and rehearse, admin to import. The token's owner needs studio.script_library to rehearse and to read data for test data, and studio.plugin_studio to import. Give the token the Global ADOM: the Builder then sees the datasets of every ADOM its owner may enter. A token bound to one ADOM sees only that ADOM's datasets. My tokens says which one each link is and how many datasets it reaches.
  3. In SATOM Builder an administrator adds the target (your SATOM's URL); each author adds their token under My tokens.
  4. Register the Builder's publisher key in SATOM (from the Builder's Publisher key page), so its packages read as signed.

Step 2 — a project#

Projects → New project: a kind, a name, a slug, an icon (the grid button opens every Bootstrap icon a plugin may use, with a search), the target and the SATOM ADOM (Auto: from the datasets it reads). The three kinds are offered as cards that say what each one is:

Kind What it is For Example
View A page in SATOM (Custom Views) that reads SATOM's data — every dataset: the device cache (FortiGate rules and addresses, FortiWeb policies, FortiADC pools…), the fleet, the administrator datasets — and shows it, filtered by input parameters such as an IP. It never changes anything. Built in Report Studio. search, look up, report, list Which firewall rules use this IP?
Widget A view sized for a dashboard tile. Built in Report Studio. a count, a status, a short list Server policies without a WAF profile: 3
App A Plugin Studio app: a form and a diagram of steps that do things — call an API, read and write data stores, run a sandboxed script, act on appliances, ask for approval. It cannot read SATOM's datasets. requests and workflows that create or change something Publish a site: reserve the IP in DDI, create the FortiWeb policy, ask for approval

Rule of thumb: show or search what SATOM already knows → a view (or a widget on a dashboard); do something — create, change, call another system, ask for approval → an app. Report Studio's editor and Plugin Studio's New app show this where you choose, and SATOM Builder uses the same words.

Already in SATOM? Projects → Open from SATOM lists every Plugin Studio app of the target and the Report Studio plugins of your token's ADOM, says which ones are already your projects, and opens the others in one click (Open selected, Open all): each is fetched as SATOM's Export writes it — unsigned, connections without their secrets — and becomes a project on that target. A script app, a code plugin, or a Report Studio plugin when your SATOM account is not a super-admin are listed with the reason instead. SATOM 4.7.0 or later; Adopt a package still takes an exported file.

The kind can be changed later in the project settings (the draft keeps everything; only the new kind's parts are packaged). Projects searches names, slugs and descriptions and filters by kind, target, ADOM and last check; the eye next to a name shows what the project is for.

The editor opens with tabs for the kind: Files, Datasets, Params, Preview (views) or Form, Diagram, Actions, Stores, Connections, API Catalog, Design, Scripts (apps), plus Test data, Database, Test run, Assistant and Raw JSON.

Step 3 — pick datasets (views)#

The Datasets tab lists every dataset your token reaches — the built-in ones, the ones your administrators published (admin_…) and one per device-object type (fortiweb_vip…) — grouped by ADOM: first Every ADOM (the basics), then one group per product, searchable. Tick the ones the view reads. Missing one? Ask an administrator to build a plugin dataset; Refresh from SATOM shows it once published. The Library page lists the same catalogue with every column, masked ones marked, relations and how each is built.

You never pick an ADOM. A plugin installs in the ADOM of the datasets it reads, and the editor's header says where: Installs in: ADOM FortiGate (auto) for a view that reads only FortiGate datasets, Installs in: Global (auto) for one that reads two products — FortiGate rules next to FortiWeb interfaces, say — which SATOM's Global console then opens (each user sees the rows of the ADOMs they may enter). The badge changes as you tick datasets; click it to read why and, with a Global token, to fix the ADOM by hand (Project details → Installs in). Check, Validate, Rehearse, Import and test data all run in that ADOM; Generate and the assistant look in Global, so the AI may pick any product's datasets. With a token bound to one ADOM, the tab lists the datasets SATOM has in other ADOMs apart, with the ADOM that holds each, so neither the editor nor the assistant claims they do not exist; SATOM refuses a package that would install where one of its datasets is missing instead of installing it broken.

Step 4 — test data from SATOM#

Open Test data. A new project starts from SATOM's own data: the rows SATOM shows you (your ADOM, your devices, sensitive columns masked) for the datasets the view reads, SATOM's built-in ones, the data stores the project uses and the lists of SATOM objects. Every table says where its rows came from. You can edit any cell, load a CSV, or Generate synthetic rows instead. These rows stay on the Builder: never in a package, never sent to the AI.

Step 5 — explore it as a database#

The Database tab shows the test data as tables (a dataset by its key, a data store as store_<slug>) in a diagram with the relations SATOM describes (to the fleet, to a parent object, to the type a field is named after). Click a table for its columns and, for a dataset, the query SATOM fills it with. More of SATOM's data adds any other dataset of the target to the test data to explore it. The SQL console runs read-only SQLite over all of it:

SELECT f.name AS device, COUNT(*) AS policies
FROM server_policies_full p JOIN fleet_appliances f ON f.id = p.appliance_id
GROUP BY f.name ORDER BY policies DESC

Step 6 — ask the assistant#

The Assistant tab keeps conversations per project, with files and images. It knows the project's draft, SATOM's rules, the target's names and the test database's tables, columns, counts and relations — never a row — so ask "which policies have no WAF profile?" and get a query to run in the Database tab, or "make this a table with a badge per status" and get a draft to apply.

Generate with AI on the project's page keeps your conversations too — the same ones the editor's AI window shows: open one to read each request and what the AI answered, see what it did, apply a result or continue it.

View or app? SATOM's data — FortiGate rules, FortiWeb objects, every dataset — is read by views and widgets. An app (a form and a diagram) has no step that reads a dataset, so "look an IP up in the FortiGate rules" is a view with an input parameter (the IP). Asked in an app, the AI says so instead of claiming the data does not exist.

Before Generate calls a view done, the Builder renders it with SATOM's own runtime over test rows that have exactly each dataset's columns, and flags a {% set %} inside a {% for %} that is read after the loop (Jinja keeps the old value): both go back to the AI to fix, with the columns of the datasets it reads — SATOM's rules check that a template parses, not that it works.

Step 7 — test run#

Test run renders the view with SATOM's own renderer and frame, walks an app's diagram on the test data (store writes change a copy you may keep), or runs a script in SATOM's jail with SATOM's SDK — on the Builder, with no network. Every run is kept.

Step 8 — to SATOM#

  1. Check — SATOM's rules, locally.
  2. Validate on SATOM — the target checks it; nothing is written.
  3. Rehearse — the target walks the app unarmed against its own objects, or renders the view with its real data, for your token.
  4. Import — into a test SATOM; it lands in draft or testing.
  5. Production: Download package and import it there, or import through a production target with a token that may import. A view's package carries the definitions of the administrator datasets it reads; a SATOM without them creates them pending its administrator's approval.

→ The full manual: SATOM Builder and the Builder's own user guide; the API it uses: SATOM API.
